quiz.title: Definite Integrals Quiz (Exercise 7.9)
quiz.intro: Eight questions on evaluating definite integrals using the fundamental theorem, applying limits and substitution with changed limits. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Evaluating definite integrals by the fundamental theorem of calculus

questions.q: Evaluate the definite integral of x dx from 1 to 3.
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of x is x²/2. Applying limits: (9/2) − (1/2) = 8/2 = 4.

questions.q: What is the value of the integral of cos x dx from 0 to π/2?
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of cos x is sin x. So sin(π/2) − sin(0) = 1 − 0 = 1.

questions.q: The fundamental theorem of calculus lets you evaluate the integral of f(x) from a to b as:
questions.explanation: If F is an antiderivative of f, the definite integral equals F(b) − F(a) — the upper limit value minus the lower limit value.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral of 3x² dx from 0 to 2.
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of 3x² is x³. Applying limits: (2)³ − (0)³ = 8 − 0 = 8.

questions.q: When substituting t = x² to evaluate the integral of 2x dx from x = 0 to x = 2, the new limits for t are:
questions.explanation: In definite integrals you change the limits to the new variable. At x = 0, t = 0; at x = 2, t = 2² = 4. So t runs from 0 to 4.

questions.q: Evaluate the integral of e^x dx from 0 to 1.
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of e^x is e^x. So e¹ − e&sup0; = e − 1.

questions.q: What is the value of the integral of 1/x dx from 1 to e?
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|. So ln(e) − ln(1) = 1 − 0 = 1.

questions.q: The integral of sin x dx from 0 to π equals:
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of sin x is −cos x. So [−cos π] − [−cos 0] = −(−1) − (−1) = 1 + 1 = 2.

faq.q: What does Exercise 7.9 of Class 12 Maths cover?
faq.a: Exercise 7.9 is about evaluating definite integrals using the fundamental theorem of calculus. You find an antiderivative, then substitute the upper and lower limits and subtract, sometimes changing the limits when you use substitution.

faq.q: How is a definite integral different from an indefinite integral?
faq.a: An indefinite integral gives a family of functions plus a constant C, while a definite integral gives a single number. Because you subtract the value at the lower limit from the value at the upper limit, the constant C cancels out and never appears in the final answer.

faq.q: Do I need to change the limits when using substitution?
faq.a: Yes, if you keep working in the new variable. When you set t = g(x), convert both limits: compute t at the lower and upper x-values and integrate between those. Alternatively you can substitute back to x before applying the original limits.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in Exercise 7.9?
faq.a: Forgetting to change the limits after substitution, or applying them in the wrong order. Always subtract the lower-limit value from the upper-limit value — reversing them flips the sign of the whole answer.
